question: Když čokoláda po čase zbělá a pokryje se šedobílým povlakem, je to plíseň a měla by se vyhodit. Pravda, nebo nepravda?
source_excerpt: Chocolate that has 'bloomed' is still safe to eat, but may have an unappetizing appearance and surface texture.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone has found a forgotten chocolate bar in the cupboard with a white coating and thrown it away as mouldy. Learning that it is just the chocolate's own fat or sugar, and that the bar is safe, overturns a common everyday assumption.
extra.verification_notes: White/grey coating on chocolate is fat or sugar bloom, not mold, and is safe to eat, so 'Nepravda' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate_bloom).

explanation: Ten povlak je obvykle kakaové máslo nebo cukr, které při změnách teploty či vlhkosti vystoupí na povrch. Čokoláda je dál bezpečná, jen ztratí lesk a trochu i chuť.

question: Mentolové bonbony Hašlerky nesou jméno skutečného člověka. Čím se ten muž živil, když mu měly bonbony pomáhat hlavně na krk?
source_excerpt: Czech singer, actor, songwriter and cabaret performer. The herbal sweets "Hašlerky" were named after him.

extra.why_interesting: Every Czech has had Hašlerky from a petrol station or a grandmother's handbag, but few stop to think the name belongs to a real person. Players assume it is just a made-up brand name. The throat clue lets them reason toward a singer, and the reveal links a household sweet to a beloved Prague chansonnier.
extra.verification_notes: Hašlerky are named after the real cabaret singer Karel Hašler, who lent his name to a throat-soothing herbal/mint candy; singer is accurate (he was also an actor and songwriter) - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_Ha%C5%A1ler

explanation: Jsou pojmenované po Karlu Hašlerovi, slavném pražském písničkáři a herci. Ostré mentolové bonbony měly chránit jeho hlas, a tak se jim dodnes říká podle něj.
